Take-home Exercise 1: Visual Analytics for Data Discovery

Author

Cao Jinming

Published

May 20, 2026

Modified

May 24, 2026

1 Overview

This report applies visual analytics to a real-world motor insurance portfolio from a Spanish non-life insurer. The exercise brief asks for R-based visual analytics that go beyond dashboard reporting and help discover factors linked to portfolio profitability and volatility.

The report is organised in the following structure: context first, analytical sandbox, data preparation, univariate exploration, bivariate analysis, statistical validation, and final findings. The analysis uses the Mendeley motor portfolio data.

Two analytical definitions are used throughout the report:

  • Profitability is measured by aggregate profit = total_premium - total_incurred and by aggregate loss_ratio = total_incurred / total_premium. Lower loss ratio indicates better underwriting profitability before expenses.
  • Volatility is measured by claim occurrence, claim frequency, capped individual loss ratio, high-loss policy rate, and upper-tail loss-ratio behaviour.

The main question is: which portfolio segments show weaker profitability or higher volatility, and are those patterns visually and statistically defensible?

2 Analytical sandbox

2.1 R packages and helper functions

The analytical sandbox uses tidyverse for data wrangling, ggplot2 and extensions for visual analytics, and knitr for tabular reporting. Reusable import and portfolio-summary functions are stored in TH_Ex/th_ex1_common.R so that the report and slides can use the same definitions.

library(tidyverse)
library(readxl)
library(scales)
library(patchwork)
library(knitr)
library(ggrepel)

if (file.exists("TH_Ex/th_ex1_common.R")) {
  source("TH_Ex/th_ex1_common.R")
} else {
  source("th_ex1_common.R")
}

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))

The table below documents the packages and helper functions used in this report, including the self-created functions stored in TH_Ex/th_ex1_common.R.

2.2 Data source and import

The dataset is the open-access motor insurance portfolio from Mendeley Data. The helper function downloads and extracts the data if the CSV and data dictionary are not already available locally. The CSV is semicolon-delimited.

dict <- read_excel(th1_dict_path)

2.3 Portfolio size and derived variables

The imported portfolio contains policy-year records from 2022 to 2024. The table below documents the derived variables and summary functions used to construct the portfolio-size table.

derived_variable_reference <- tribble(
  ~type, ~name, ~purpose,
  "Derived variable", "profit", "Measures underwriting result at policy-year level: total premium minus total incurred loss.",
  "Derived variable", "loss_ratio", "Measures loss burden relative to premium: total incurred loss divided by total premium.",
  "Derived variable", "loss_ratio_cap", "Caps individual loss ratio at the 99th percentile so plots are not dominated by extreme outliers.",
  "Derived variable", "claim_flag", "Marks whether a policy-year has at least one claim; used for claim-record share and volatility checks.",
  "Derived variable", "claim_frequency", "Standardises claim count by exposure: total claims divided by total exposure.",
  "Derived variable", "severity", "Measures average incurred loss per claim; defined only for records with at least one claim.",
  "Derived variable", "driver_age_band", "Groups driver age into bands for segment-level profitability and volatility comparison.",
  "Derived variable", "vehicle_age_band", "Groups vehicle age into bands for segment-level profitability and volatility comparison.",
  "Summary table", "portfolio_size", "Stores the headline portfolio-size, premium, incurred loss, profit, loss-ratio, and claim-share metrics displayed in this section."
)

portfolio_size <- tibble(
  measure = c(
    "Policy-year records",
    "Distinct insured IDs",
    "Calendar years",
    "Variables after derivation",
    "Aggregate premium",
    "Aggregate incurred loss",
    "Aggregate profit",
    "Aggregate loss ratio",
    "Claim-record share"
  ),
  value = c(
    comma(nrow(motor)),
    comma(n_distinct(motor$insured_id)),
    paste(levels(motor$year), collapse = ", "),
    comma(ncol(motor)),
    money(sum(motor$total_premium, na.rm = TRUE)),
    money(sum(motor$total_incurred, na.rm = TRUE)),
    money(sum(motor$profit, na.rm = TRUE)),
    pct(sum(motor$total_incurred, na.rm = TRUE) / sum(motor$total_premium, na.rm = TRUE)),
    pct(mean(motor$claim_flag, na.rm = TRUE))
  )
)

  • Portfolio is profitable in aggregate before expenses.
  • Aggregate totals can hide segment-level volatility.
  • The remaining analysis focuses on distributions, outliers, and segment comparisons.

2.4 Data quality checks

missing_tbl <- motor |>
  summarise(across(everything(), ~sum(is.na(.x)))) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable", values_to = "missing_records") |>
  filter(missing_records > 0) |>
  mutate(missing_share = missing_records / nrow(motor)) |>
  arrange(desc(missing_records))

kable(missing_tbl, digits = 4)
variable missing_records missing_share
severity 303333 0.8565
fuel_type 1287 0.0036
vehicle_value 513 0.0014
loss_ratio 49 0.0001
loss_ratio_cap 49 0.0001
claim_frequency 49 0.0001
vehicle_age 2 0.0000
age_driving_licence 2 0.0000
vehicle_age_band 2 0.0000
  • Core premium and incurred-loss variables are mostly complete.
  • severity has many missing values because it is defined only for claim records.
  • Missing fuel_type, vehicle_value, vehicle_age, and age_driving_licence records are retained to avoid distorting exposure totals.

3 Task 1: Univariate visual analytics

This section applies the recommended univariate visual for each source column in the motor insurance portfolio. The approach is type-specific:

  • identifiers are summarised with uniqueness and duplicate counts, not plotted as continuous numbers;
  • categorical variables use count/composition bars, with top-N grouping for high-cardinality fields;
  • ordinary numerical variables use a histogram plus boxplot;
  • optional premium and incurred-loss variables are split into zero-versus-positive bars plus positive-value distributions;
  • claim counts use count bars and a separate 0-claim versus 1-or-more-claims view.

3.1 Recommended visual plan

motor_profile <- motor |>
  mutate(
    year_numeric = as.numeric(as.character(year)),
    licence_years_held = if_else(
      !is.na(year_numeric) & !is.na(age_driving_licence),
      year_numeric - age_driving_licence,
      NA_real_
    )
  )

age_driving_licence Year variable Histogram or bar chart by licence year When drivers got their licence.
licence_years_held Derived numerical Histogram + boxplot Approximate driving experience, calculated as year minus licence year.
fuel_type Categorical Bar chart Diesel versus gasoline split.
vehicle_value Numerical money/value Histogram + boxplot plus missing-value check Car value distribution, missing values, and expensive outliers.
seats Discrete numerical / categorical Bar chart Common seat numbers, for example 4, 5, or 7.
power_to_weight_ratio Numerical Histogram + boxplot Vehicle performance distribution and outliers.
vehicle_brand High-cardinality categorical Horizontal bar chart of top 20 brands Most common brands; rare brands are grouped as Other.
municipality_type Categorical Bar chart Inland, coastal, and island distribution.
circulation_area Categorical Bar chart Urban versus rural distribution.
total_premium Numerical money Histogram + boxplot Overall price distribution and expensive policies.
liability_premium Numerical money Histogram + boxplot Cost of third-party liability coverage.
property_damage_premium Numerical money Histogram + boxplot Distribution of property damage premium.
theft_premium Optional premium Zero-versus-positive bar plus histogram of positive premiums Whether theft coverage is commonly purchased.
fire_premium Optional premium Zero-versus-positive bar plus histogram of positive premiums Whether fire coverage is commonly purchased.
glass_premium Optional premium Zero-versus-positive bar plus histogram of positive premiums Whether glass coverage is common.
legal_protection_premium Optional premium Zero-versus-positive bar plus histogram of positive premiums Whether legal protection is commonly purchased.
occupants_premium Optional premium Zero-versus-positive bar plus histogram of positive premiums Whether occupant injury coverage is common.
total_claims Count Bar chart of claim-count values plus 0 versus 1+ claims Usually many policies have 0 claims.
liability_claims Count Bar chart of claim-count values plus 0 versus 1+ claims Number of liability claims.
liability_property_claims Count Bar chart of claim-count values plus 0 versus 1+ claims Claims involving third-party property damage.
liability_injury_claims Count Bar chart of claim-count values plus 0 versus 1+ claims Injury-related liability claims.
property_claims Count Bar chart of claim-count values plus 0 versus 1+ claims Property damage claim frequency.
theft_claims Count Bar chart of claim-count values plus 0 versus 1+ claims Theft claim frequency.
fire_claims Count Bar chart of claim-count values plus 0 versus 1+ claims Fire claim frequency.
glass_claims Count Bar chart of claim-count values plus 0 versus 1+ claims Glass claim frequency.
legal_protection_claims Count Bar chart of claim-count values plus 0 versus 1+ claims Legal protection claim frequency.
occupants_claims Count Bar chart of claim-count values plus 0 versus 1+ claims Occupant injury claim frequency.
total_incurred Numerical money Zero-versus-positive bar; log-scale histogram and boxplot for positive values Claim cost severity and extreme losses.
liability_incurred Numerical money Zero-versus-positive bar; log-scale histogram and boxplot for positive values Cost of liability claims.
liability_property_incurred Numerical money Zero-versus-positive bar; log-scale histogram and boxplot for positive values Cost of liability property damage.
liability_injury_incurred Numerical money Zero-versus-positive bar; log-scale histogram and boxplot for positive values Injury claim costs, likely very skewed.
property_incurred Numerical money Zero-versus-positive bar; log-scale histogram and boxplot for positive values Property damage claim costs.
theft_incurred Numerical money Zero-versus-positive bar; log-scale histogram and boxplot for positive values Theft claim costs.
fire_incurred Numerical money Zero-versus-positive bar; log-scale histogram and boxplot for positive values Fire claim costs.
glass_incurred Numerical money Zero-versus-positive bar; log-scale histogram and boxplot for positive values Glass claim costs.
legal_protection_incurred Numerical money Zero-versus-positive bar; log-scale histogram and boxplot for positive values Legal protection claim costs.
occupants_incurred Numerical money Zero-versus-positive bar; log-scale histogram and boxplot for positive values Occupant injury claim costs.
total_exposure Numerical Histogram + boxplot Full-year policies versus partial-year policies; check values above 1.
liability_exposure Numerical Histogram + boxplot Exposure time for liability coverage.

Observations

  • The visual choice is now tied to the analytical type of each column, rather than only to its stored R class.
  • Optional coverages and incurred-loss fields are separated into zero-versus-positive and positive-value severity views to avoid zero inflation hiding the useful distribution.
  • licence_years_held is added as a derived check because it is easier to interpret than the raw licence year alone.

3.2 Reusable profiling functions

format_profile_value <- function(x, var = NULL) {
  if (length(x) == 0 || is.na(x) || !is.finite(x)) return("NA")
  if (!is.null(var) && str_detect(var, "premium|incurred|vehicle_value|profit|severity")) {
    return(money(x))
  }
  comma(round(x, 2))
}

numeric_profile_summary <- function(df, var) {
  x <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(df[[var]]))
  finite_x <- x[is.finite(x)]
  tibble(
    metric = c("Missing records", "Missing share", "Zero share", "Minimum", "Median", "Mean", "95th percentile", "Maximum"),
    value = c(
      comma(sum(is.na(x))),
      pct(mean(is.na(x))),
      if (length(finite_x) == 0) "NA" else pct(mean(finite_x == 0)),
      if (length(finite_x) == 0) "NA" else format_profile_value(min(finite_x), var),
      if (length(finite_x) == 0) "NA" else format_profile_value(median(finite_x), var),
      if (length(finite_x) == 0) "NA" else format_profile_value(mean(finite_x), var),
      if (length(finite_x) == 0) "NA" else format_profile_value(quantile(finite_x, 0.95, na.rm = TRUE), var),
      if (length(finite_x) == 0) "NA" else format_profile_value(max(finite_x), var)
    )
  )
}

categorical_profile_summary <- function(df, var) {
  x <- df[[var]]
  non_missing <- x[!is.na(x)]
  tab <- sort(table(non_missing), decreasing = TRUE)
  tibble(
    metric = c("Missing records", "Missing share", "Distinct non-missing values", "Top category", "Top-category share"),
    value = c(
      comma(sum(is.na(x))),
      pct(mean(is.na(x))),
      comma(n_distinct(x, na.rm = TRUE)),
      if (length(tab) == 0) "NA" else names(tab)[1],
      if (length(tab) == 0) "NA" else pct(as.numeric(tab[1]) / length(non_missing))
    )
  )
}

id_profile_summary <- function(df, var) {
  x <- df[[var]]
  tibble(
    metric = c("Policy-year records", "Unique IDs", "Duplicate ID records", "Missing ID records"),
    value = c(
      comma(length(x)),
      comma(n_distinct(x, na.rm = TRUE)),
      comma(length(x) - n_distinct(x, na.rm = TRUE)),
      comma(sum(is.na(x)))
    )
  )
}

profile_summary <- function(df, var, family) {
  if (family == "id") return(id_profile_summary(df, var))
  if (family %in% c("categorical", "ordinal", "year")) return(categorical_profile_summary(df, var))
  numeric_profile_summary(df, var)
}

empty_plot <- function(title, message) {
  ggplot() +
    annotate("text", x = 0, y = 0, label = message) +
    theme_void() +
    labs(title = title)
}

hist_box_visual <- function(df, var, title = NULL, subtitle = NULL, positive_only = FALSE, log_scale = FALSE) {
  plot_df <- tibble(value = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(df[[var]]))) |>
    filter(is.finite(value))
  if (positive_only) plot_df <- plot_df |> filter(value > 0)

  if (nrow(plot_df) == 0) {
    return(empty_plot(paste("Distribution of", var), "No finite values available"))
  }

  if (!log_scale) {
    lower <- quantile(plot_df$value, 0.01, na.rm = TRUE)
    upper <- quantile(plot_df$value, 0.99, na.rm = TRUE)
    plot_df <- plot_df |>
      mutate(value_plot = pmin(pmax(value, lower), upper))
    plot_subtitle <- coalesce(subtitle, "Histogram and boxplot; values are capped at the 1st and 99th percentiles for readability only.")
  } else {
    plot_df <- plot_df |> mutate(value_plot = value)
    plot_subtitle <- coalesce(subtitle, "Positive values only; x-axis is log-scaled to reveal skewed claim-cost severity.")
  }

  x_labeller <- if (str_detect(var, "premium|incurred|vehicle_value|profit|severity")) money else comma

  hist <- ggplot(plot_df, aes(x = value_plot)) +
    geom_histogram(bins = 35, colour = "white", fill = "#2c7fb8") +
    labs(x = var, y = "Number of records") +
    scale_x_continuous(labels = x_labeller)

  box <- ggplot(plot_df, aes(x = value_plot, y = "")) +
    geom_boxplot(fill = "#a6bddb", colour = "#045a8d", outlier.alpha = 0.35) +
    labs(x = var, y = NULL) +
    scale_x_continuous(labels = x_labeller)

  if (log_scale) {
    hist <- hist + scale_x_log10(labels = x_labeller)
    box <- box + scale_x_log10(labels = x_labeller)
  }

  hist / box +
    plot_layout(heights = c(3, 1)) +
    plot_annotation(
      title = coalesce(title, paste("Distribution of", var)),
      subtitle = plot_subtitle
    )
}

zero_positive_bar <- function(df, var, positive_label = "Positive") {
  fill_values <- c("#bdbdbd", "#2c7fb8", "#fdae6b", "#756bb1")
  names(fill_values) <- c("Zero", positive_label, "Negative", "Missing")

  tibble(value = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(df[[var]]))) |>
    mutate(status = case_when(
      is.na(value) ~ "Missing",
      value > 0 ~ positive_label,
      value == 0 ~ "Zero",
      TRUE ~ "Negative"
    )) |>
    count(status, name = "n") |>
    mutate(
      share = n / sum(n),
      status = factor(status, levels = c("Zero", positive_label, "Negative", "Missing"))
    ) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = status, y = share, fill = status)) +
    geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
    geom_text(aes(label = percent(share, accuracy = 0.1)), vjust = -0.25, size = 3.5) +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = percent, limits = c(0, NA)) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = fill_values) +
    labs(
      title = paste("Zero versus positive", var),
      x = NULL,
      y = "Share of records"
    )
}

optional_premium_visual <- function(df, var) {
  zero_positive_bar(df, var, positive_label = "Positive premium") /
    hist_box_visual(
      df, var,
      title = paste("Positive premium distribution for", var),
      subtitle = "Positive premium values only; zero premiums are shown separately above.",
      positive_only = TRUE,
      log_scale = FALSE
    ) +
    plot_layout(heights = c(1, 2.4))
}

incurred_visual <- function(df, var) {
  zero_positive_bar(df, var, positive_label = "Positive incurred") /
    hist_box_visual(
      df, var,
      title = paste("Positive incurred-cost distribution for", var),
      positive_only = TRUE,
      log_scale = TRUE
    ) +
    plot_layout(heights = c(1, 2.4))
}

claim_count_visual <- function(df, var) {
  count_plot <- tibble(value = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(df[[var]]))) |>
    mutate(claim_count = if_else(is.na(value), "Missing", as.character(value))) |>
    count(claim_count, name = "n") |>
    mutate(claim_count = fct_reorder(claim_count, suppressWarnings(as.numeric(claim_count)), .na_rm = TRUE)) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = claim_count, y = n)) +
    geom_col(fill = "#2c7fb8") +
    labs(
      title = paste("Claim-count distribution for", var),
      x = "Claim count",
      y = "Number of records"
    )

  flag_plot <- tibble(value = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(df[[var]]))) |>
    mutate(status = case_when(
      is.na(value) ~ "Missing",
      value == 0 ~ "0 claims",
      value > 0 ~ "1 or more claims",
      TRUE ~ "Negative"
    )) |>
    count(status, name = "n") |>
    mutate(
      share = n / sum(n),
      status = factor(status, levels = c("0 claims", "1 or more claims", "Negative", "Missing"))
    ) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = status, y = share, fill = status)) +
    geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
    geom_text(aes(label = percent(share, accuracy = 0.1)), vjust = -0.25, size = 3.5) +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = percent, limits = c(0, NA)) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c("0 claims" = "#bdbdbd", "1 or more claims" = "#2c7fb8", "Negative" = "#fdae6b", "Missing" = "#756bb1")) +
    labs(
      title = paste("Claim occurrence for", var),
      x = NULL,
      y = "Share of records"
    )

  count_plot / flag_plot + plot_layout(heights = c(1.4, 1))
}

year_visual <- function(df, var) {
  df |>
    transmute(year_value = fct_na_value_to_level(as.factor(.data[[var]]), level = "Missing")) |>
    count(year_value, name = "n") |>
    ggplot(aes(x = year_value, y = n, group = 1)) +
    geom_col(fill = "#756bb1", alpha = 0.75) +
    geom_line(colour = "#d95f0e", linewidth = 1) +
    geom_point(colour = "#d95f0e", size = 2) +
    labs(
      title = "Policy-year record counts by year",
      x = "Year",
      y = "Number of records"
    )
}

categorical_visual <- function(df, var, family = "categorical", top_n = NA_real_) {
  plot_df <- df |>
    transmute(category = fct_na_value_to_level(as.factor(.data[[var]]), level = "Missing")) |>
    count(category, name = "n")

  if (family == "ordinal" && var == "bonus_score") {
    preferred_levels <- c("bad", "Bad", "neutral", "Neutral", "good", "Good")
    level_order <- c(intersect(preferred_levels, as.character(plot_df$category)), setdiff(as.character(plot_df$category), preferred_levels))
    plot_df <- plot_df |> mutate(category = factor(as.character(category), levels = level_order))
  } else {
    if (!is.na(top_n)) {
      plot_df <- plot_df |>
        mutate(category = fct_lump_n(category, n = top_n, w = n, other_level = "Other")) |>
        group_by(category) |>
        summarise(n = sum(n), .groups = "drop")
    }
    plot_df <- plot_df |> mutate(category = fct_reorder(category, n))
  }

  plot_df |>
    mutate(share = n / sum(n)) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = category, y = share)) +
    geom_col(fill = "#756bb1") +
    coord_flip() +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = percent) +
    labs(
      title = paste("Composition of", var),
      subtitle = if (!is.na(top_n)) paste("Top", top_n, "categories retained; remaining categories grouped as Other.") else "Bars show share of policy-year records.",
      x = NULL,
      y = "Share of records"
    )
}

make_profile_visual <- function(df, spec_row) {
  var <- spec_row$variable
  family <- spec_row$visual_family
  top_n <- spec_row$top_n

  if (family == "id") return(NULL)
  if (family == "year") return(year_visual(df, var))
  if (family %in% c("categorical", "ordinal")) return(categorical_visual(df, var, family, top_n))
  if (family == "discrete") return(categorical_visual(df, var, "categorical", NA_real_))
  if (family == "optional_premium") return(optional_premium_visual(df, var))
  if (family == "incurred") return(incurred_visual(df, var))
  if (family == "claim_count") return(claim_count_visual(df, var))
  hist_box_visual(df, var)
}

profile_insights <- function(df, spec_row) {
  var <- spec_row$variable
  family <- spec_row$visual_family
  x <- df[[var]]
  bullets <- c(paste0("Recommended check: ", spec_row$what_to_look_for))

  if (family == "id") {
    duplicate_records <- length(x) - n_distinct(x, na.rm = TRUE)
    bullets <- c(
      bullets,
      paste0("There are ", comma(n_distinct(x, na.rm = TRUE)), " unique IDs across ", comma(length(x)), " policy-year records."),
      paste0("Duplicate ID records equal ", comma(duplicate_records), "; this is expected if an insured appears in more than one year, but the ID should not be modelled as a continuous value.")
    )
    return(paste0("- ", bullets, collapse = "\n") |> paste0("\n"))
  }

  if (family %in% c("categorical", "ordinal", "year", "discrete")) {
    tab <- sort(table(x, useNA = "no"), decreasing = TRUE)
    missing_share <- mean(is.na(x))
    distinct_values <- n_distinct(x, na.rm = TRUE)
    if (missing_share > 0) bullets <- c(bullets, paste0("Missing records account for ", pct(missing_share), " and are shown explicitly where relevant."))
    if (distinct_values > 20) bullets <- c(bullets, paste0("The variable has ", distinct_values, " distinct values, so top-N grouping protects readability."))
    if (length(tab) > 0) bullets <- c(bullets, paste0("The largest category is `", names(tab)[1], "` with ", pct(as.numeric(tab[1]) / sum(tab)), " of non-missing records."))
  } else {
    num_x <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(x))
    finite_x <- num_x[is.finite(num_x)]
    if (length(finite_x) == 0) bullets <- c(bullets, "No finite values are available for interpretation.")
    if (length(finite_x) > 0) {
      missing_share <- mean(is.na(num_x))
      zero_share <- mean(finite_x == 0)
      median_value <- median(finite_x)
      mean_value <- mean(finite_x)
      p95_value <- quantile(finite_x, 0.95, na.rm = TRUE)
      max_value <- max(finite_x)
      if (missing_share > 0) bullets <- c(bullets, paste0("Missing records account for ", pct(missing_share), "."))
      if (zero_share > 0.50) bullets <- c(bullets, paste0("The variable is zero-inflated: ", pct(zero_share), " of finite records are zero."))
      if (median_value == 0 && p95_value > 0) {
        bullets <- c(bullets, "The median is zero but the upper tail is positive, so the positive-value visual is more informative than a standard histogram alone.")
      } else if (abs(mean_value) > abs(median_value) * 2 && p95_value > median_value) {
        bullets <- c(bullets, "The mean is much larger than the median, indicating right skew and possible expensive outliers.")
      }
      bullets <- c(bullets, paste0("The 95th percentile is ", format_profile_value(p95_value, var), " and the maximum is ", format_profile_value(max_value, var), "."))
    }
  }

  if (length(bullets) > 3) bullets <- bullets[1:3]
  paste0("- ", bullets, collapse = "\n") |> paste0("\n")
}

3.3 Column-by-column profiles

for (i in seq_len(nrow(profile_spec))) {
  spec_row <- profile_spec[i, ]
  var <- spec_row$variable
  family <- spec_row$visual_family

  cat("\n\n#### `", var, "`\n\n", sep = "")
  cat("**Variable type:** ", spec_row$variable_type, "  \n", sep = "")
  cat("**Best univariate visual:** ", spec_row$best_univariate_visual, "\n\n", sep = "")

  print(profile_summary(motor_profile, var, family) |> kable())
  cat("\n\n")

  plot_obj <- make_profile_visual(motor_profile, spec_row)
  if (is.null(plot_obj)) {
    cat("No normal numeric plot is shown because this is an identifier field.\n\n")
  } else {
    print(plot_obj)
    cat("\n\n")
  }

  cat("::: {.observation-box}\n")
  cat("**Insights**\n\n")
  cat(profile_insights(motor_profile, spec_row))
  cat(":::\n\n")
}

3.3.1 insured_id

Variable type: ID
Best univariate visual: Uniqueness count and duplicate count

metric value

Unique IDs 185,678
Duplicate ID records 168,462
Missing ID records 0

No normal numeric plot is shown because this is an identifier field.

  • Recommended check: How many unique policies or customers exist; do not treat this as a normal numeric variable.

4 Task 2: Bivariate visual analytics and validation

Bivariate analysis compares profitability and volatility across time and major risk-related segments. The main profitability visual is aggregate loss ratio; the main volatility visuals are claim frequency, high-loss rate, and spread of capped individual loss ratios.

4.1 Temporal trend: profitability worsens in 2024

yearly <- portfolio_summary(motor, year)
kable(yearly, digits = 3)
year records exposure premium incurred claims profit high_loss_rate p95_loss_ratio loss_ratio claim_frequency avg_premium avg_severity
2022 67172 41912.50 18697928 12270105 12665 6427823 0.080 2.419 0.656 0.302 446.118 968.820
2023 118835 82399.04 35344308 23488354 25158 11855954 0.087 2.744 0.665 0.305 428.941 933.634
2024 168133 126014.36 51037433 38106351 39276 12931082 0.097 3.205 0.747 0.312 405.013 970.220
  • The year-level table summarises exposure, premium, incurred loss, profit, and loss ratio.
  • It provides the numeric baseline for the temporal trend plot.
trend_amount <- yearly |>
  select(year, Premium = premium, Incurred = incurred, Profit = profit) |>
  pivot_longer(-year, names_to = "measure", values_to = "amount") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = amount, colour = measure, group = measure)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = money) +
  labs(
    title = "Premium, incurred loss, and profit by year",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Aggregate amount"
  )

trend_lr <- yearly |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = loss_ratio, group = 1)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, colour = "#d95f0e") +
  geom_point(size = 3, colour = "#d95f0e") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = pct) +
  labs(
    title = "Aggregate loss ratio by year",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Loss ratio"
  )

trend_amount + trend_lr + plot_layout(widths = c(1.4, 1))
  • Premium and incurred losses both increase over time.
  • Incurred losses grow faster in 2024.
  • The 2024 loss-ratio rise indicates weaker profitability despite positive aggregate profit.

4.2 Policy type: comprehensive covers carry higher risk

policy_tbl <- portfolio_summary(motor, policy_type) |>
  arrange(desc(loss_ratio))

kable(policy_tbl, digits = 3)
policy_type records exposure premium incurred claims profit high_loss_rate p95_loss_ratio loss_ratio claim_frequency avg_premium avg_severity
COMP_N 16181 12342.351 10344550 9709280.8 12907 635269.3 0.208 4.546 0.939 1.046 838.135 752.249
COMP_E 91199 65040.337 35712392 26367075.6 26687 9345316.3 0.116 3.335 0.738 0.410 549.081 988.012
TPG 36367 24905.351 8201409 5671461.2 5156 2529947.8 0.070 2.235 0.692 0.207 329.303 1099.973
CC 204636 144235.186 49801769 31563558.5 31842 18238210.8 0.074 2.497 0.634 0.221 345.282 991.256
TP 5757 3802.674 1019549 553434.5 507 466114.6 0.047 0.177 0.543 0.133 268.114 1091.587
  • The policy-type table ranks products by aggregate loss ratio.
  • It separates product profitability from individual policy-year spread.
policy_lr <- policy_tbl |>
  mutate(policy_type = fct_reorder(policy_type, loss_ratio)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = policy_type, y = loss_ratio, fill = policy_type)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "red") +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = pct) +
  labs(
    title = "Aggregate loss ratio by policy type",
    subtitle = "Dashed line marks break-even before expenses.",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Loss ratio"
  )

policy_box <- motor |>
  filter(!is.na(policy_type), !is.na(loss_ratio_cap)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = fct_reorder(policy_type, loss_ratio_cap, .fun = median), y = loss_ratio_cap)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "#9ecae1", outlier.alpha = 0.06) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = pct) +
  labs(
    title = "Spread of capped individual loss ratio",
    subtitle = "Capping exposes group spread without letting extreme outliers dominate.",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Capped individual loss ratio"
  )

policy_lr + policy_box
  • COMP_N has the weakest aggregate profitability, followed by COMP_E.
  • Most policy-year records still have zero or low individual loss ratios.
  • Weak segment performance is driven by claim frequency and upper-tail losses, not by every policy performing poorly.

4.3 Segment scan: bonus score, fuel type, and circulation area

seg_long <- bind_rows(
  portfolio_summary(motor, bonus_score) |>
    mutate(segment = "Bonus score", category = as.character(bonus_score)),
  portfolio_summary(motor, fuel_type) |>
    mutate(segment = "Fuel type", category = fct_na_value_to_level(as.factor(fuel_type), "Missing") |> as.character()),
  portfolio_summary(motor, circulation_area) |>
    mutate(segment = "Circulation area", category = as.character(circulation_area)),
  portfolio_summary(motor, payment_frequency) |>
    mutate(segment = "Payment frequency", category = as.character(payment_frequency))
)

seg_long |>
  mutate(category = fct_reorder(category, loss_ratio)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = category, y = loss_ratio, fill = segment)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "red") +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = pct) +
  facet_wrap(~ segment, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    title = "Loss ratio differs across risk-related categories",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Aggregate loss ratio"
  )
  • Non-good bonus scores, diesel vehicles, urban circulation, and non-annual payment frequencies show higher loss ratios.
  • These segments are useful screening candidates for underwriting review.
  • The visual signals are not causal by themselves because exposure, product mix, and vehicle profiles can differ.

4.4 Driver and vehicle age bands

age_driver <- portfolio_summary(motor, driver_age_band) |>
  mutate(segment = "Driver age", category = as.character(driver_age_band))
age_vehicle <- portfolio_summary(motor, vehicle_age_band) |>
  mutate(segment = "Vehicle age", category = as.character(vehicle_age_band))

bind_rows(age_driver, age_vehicle) |>
  filter(!is.na(category)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = category, y = loss_ratio, group = segment, colour = segment)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = pct) +
  facet_wrap(~ segment, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(
    title = "Loss ratio by driver-age and vehicle-age bands",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Aggregate loss ratio"
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
  • Driver-age and vehicle-age bands show visible differences in loss ratio.
  • The patterns are not perfectly monotonic.
  • Age bands are useful segmentation variables, but not standalone explanations of risk.

4.5 Policy type by year heatmap

motor |>
  group_by(year, policy_type) |>
  summarise(
    exposure = sum(total_exposure, na.rm = TRUE),
    premium = sum(total_premium, na.rm = TRUE),
    incurred = sum(total_incurred, na.rm = TRUE),
    loss_ratio = incurred / premium,
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = policy_type, fill = loss_ratio)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = pct(loss_ratio)), colour = "white", fontface = "bold") +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#2c7fb8", high = "#d7301f", labels = pct) +
  labs(
    title = "Loss-ratio heatmap by year and policy type",
    subtitle = "Darker red cells identify combinations needing closer monitoring.",
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL,
    fill = "Loss ratio"
  )
  • The heatmap links year-level deterioration with policy-type differences.
  • Darker cells flag policy-year combinations needing closer monitoring.
  • The view helps separate persistent segment weakness from one-year deterioration.

4.6 Brand-level volatility screen

brand_tbl <- motor |>
  group_by(vehicle_brand) |>
  summarise(
    records = n(),
    exposure = sum(total_exposure, na.rm = TRUE),
    premium = sum(total_premium, na.rm = TRUE),
    incurred = sum(total_incurred, na.rm = TRUE),
    claims = sum(total_claims, na.rm = TRUE),
    loss_ratio = incurred / premium,
    claim_frequency = claims / exposure,
    high_loss_rate = mean(loss_ratio > 1, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  filter(exposure >= 1000)

brand_tbl |>
  ggplot(aes(x = claim_frequency, y = loss_ratio, size = exposure)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "red") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.65, colour = "#08519c") +
  geom_text_repel(
    data = brand_tbl |> slice_max(loss_ratio, n = 8),
    aes(label = vehicle_brand),
    size = 3,
    max.overlaps = 20
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = number_format(accuracy = 0.01)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = pct) +
  scale_size_continuous(labels = comma, range = c(2, 12)) +
  labs(
    title = "Brand-level screen for high loss ratio and claim frequency",
    subtitle = "Only brands with exposure >= 1,000 are shown.",
    x = "Claim frequency",
    y = "Aggregate loss ratio",
    size = "Exposure"
  )
  • The bubble chart screens brands by claim frequency, loss ratio, and exposure.
  • Upper-right brands combine higher claim frequency and higher loss ratio.
  • Large upper-right bubbles should be prioritised for deeper investigation.

4.7 Statistical validation

The dataset is large and skewed, so visual signals are validated with non-parametric and categorical tests:

  • Kruskal-Wallis tests check whether capped individual loss ratio differs across segment groups.
  • Chi-square tests check whether claim occurrence differs across segment groups.
  • Spearman correlations check monotonic relationships between numerical variables and capped loss ratio.
test_vars <- c(
  "policy_type", "bonus_score", "driver_age_band", "vehicle_age_band",
  "fuel_type", "circulation_area", "payment_frequency", "year"
)

kw_tbl <- map_dfr(test_vars, \(v) {
  kt <- kruskal.test(as.formula(paste("loss_ratio_cap ~", v)), data = motor)
  tibble(
    test = "Kruskal-Wallis",
    variable = v,
    statistic = unname(kt$statistic),
    p_value = kt$p.value
  )
})

chi_tbl <- map_dfr(test_vars, \(v) {
  ct <- chisq.test(table(motor[[v]], motor$claim_flag))
  tibble(
    test = "Chi-square",
    variable = v,
    statistic = unname(ct$statistic),
    p_value = ct$p.value
  )
})

validation_tbl <- bind_rows(kw_tbl, chi_tbl) |>
  mutate(p_value_label = format.pval(p_value, digits = 3)) |>
  select(test, variable, statistic, p_value_label)

kable(validation_tbl, digits = 2)

  • The p-values should be interpreted with exposure and practical effect size because the dataset is large.
corr_tbl <- map_dfr(
  c("driver_age", "vehicle_age", "age_driving_licence", "vehicle_value",
    "seats", "power_to_weight_ratio", "total_premium"),
  \(v) {
    ct <- suppressWarnings(cor.test(motor[[v]], motor$loss_ratio_cap,
                                    method = "spearman", exact = FALSE))
    tibble(variable = v, spearman_rho = unname(ct$estimate), p_value = ct$p.value)
  }
) |>
  mutate(p_value_label = format.pval(p_value, digits = 3)) |>
  arrange(desc(abs(spearman_rho)))

  • Most tests are statistically significant because the dataset is large.
  • Practical interpretation should combine visual difference, exposure, effect direction, and business relevance.
  • Total premium has the strongest monotonic relationship with capped loss ratio; most demographic and vehicle correlations are small.

5 Key findings

  1. The portfolio is profitable in aggregate but exposed to a claim-driven upper tail. Most records have no claim, but a minority of claim records strongly affects incurred loss and loss ratio.
  2. Profitability weakens in 2024. The year-level loss ratio increases, showing that incurred losses grew faster than premium.
  3. Policy type is the clearest segmentation signal. COMP_N and COMP_E have higher loss ratios than third-party-focused products, suggesting that comprehensive cover requires closer pricing and claim review.
  4. Bonus score, fuel type, circulation area, and payment frequency show meaningful differences. These variables help explain portfolio heterogeneity, but each should be interpreted together with exposure and product mix.
  5. Volatility is concentrated in tails, not medians. Boxplots, capped loss-ratio charts, and the brand bubble chart show why underwriting decisions should account for high-loss policy-year behaviour.

6 Recommendations

  • Monitor COMP_N and COMP_E separately from the rest of the portfolio because their loss-ratio and volatility profile differs materially.
  • Use the 2024 deterioration as an early-warning signal and review whether it is caused by exposure growth, claim frequency, severity, or a changing product mix.
  • Treat high-loss brand, fuel, and circulation-area segments as screening candidates for deeper underwriting review rather than as immediate pricing rules.
  • Extend the analysis with external enrichment, such as regional traffic density, weather exposure, or vehicle repair-cost indicators, to better explain the root causes of underperformance.
